claim: Nanopore direct RNA sequencing was adapted to examine RNA from wild-type Arabidopsis thaliana (Col-0) and a mutant defective in mRNA methylation (m6A).
source: We adapted nanopore direct RNA sequencing to examine RNA from a wild-type accession of the model plant Arabidopsis thaliana and a mutant defective in mRNA methylation (m6A).
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the experimental approach used in the study.

claim: m6A can be mapped in full-length mRNAs transcriptome-wide using nanopore direct RNA sequencing.
source: Here we show that m6A can be mapped in full-length mRNAs transcriptome-wide and reveal the combinatorial diversity of cap-associated transcription start sites, splicing events, poly(A) site choice and poly(A) tail length.
evidence: The abstract states this as a key finding of the study.

claim: Nanopore direct RNA sequencing reveals the combinatorial diversity of cap-associated transcription start sites, splicing events, poly(A) site choice and poly(A) tail length.
source: Here we show that m6A can be mapped in full-length mRNAs transcriptome-wide and reveal the combinatorial diversity of cap-associated transcription start sites, splicing events, poly(A) site choice and poly(A) tail length.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this as a finding from the study.

claim: Loss of m6A from 3' untranslated regions is associated with decreased relative transcript abundance.
source: Loss of m6A from 3' untranslated regions is associated with decreased relative transcript abundance and defective RNA 3′ end formation.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this association observed in the study.

claim: Loss of m6A from 3' untranslated regions is associated with defective RNA 3′ end formation.
source: Loss of m6A from 3' untranslated regions is associated with decreased relative transcript abundance and defective RNA 3′ end formation.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this association observed in the study.

claim: Disrupted m6A causes a lengthening of the circadian period.
source: A functional consequence of disrupted m6A is a lengthening of the circadian period.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this functional consequence.

claim: Nanopore direct RNA sequencing can reveal the complexity of mRNA processing and modification in full-length single molecule reads.
source: We conclude that nanopore direct RNA sequencing can reveal the complexity of mRNA processing and modification in full-length single molecule reads.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this conclusion.

claim: The findings from nanopore direct RNA sequencing can refine Arabidopsis genome annotation.
source: These findings can refine Arabidopsis genome annotation.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this potential application.

claim: Applying nanopore direct RNA sequencing to less well-studied species could transform our understanding of what their genomes encode.
source: Further, applying this approach to less well-studied species could transform our understanding of what their genomes encode.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this potential application.

claim: The most abundant internal modification of mRNA is methylation of adenosine at the N6 position (m6A).
source: The most abundant internal modification of mRNA is methylation of adenosine at the N6 position (m6A).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: RNA sequencing involves copying RNA into complementary DNA (cDNA) with reverse transcriptases (RTs) and then sequencing the subsequent DNA copies.
source: RNA sequencing (RNAseq) is used to dissect transcriptome complexity: it involves copying RNA into complementary DNA (cDNA) with reverse transcriptases (RTs) and then sequencing the subsequent DNA copies.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about RNA sequencing methodology.

claim: RNAseq limitations include misidentification of 3′ ends through internal priming.
source: RNAseq reveals diverse features of transcriptomes, but limitations can include misidentification of 3′ ends through internal priming (Jan et al., 2011), spurious antisense and splicing events produced by RT template switching (Houseley and Tollervey, 2010; Mourão et al., 2019), and the inability to detect all base modifications in the copying process (Helm and Motorin, 2017).
evidence: This limitation is cited with reference to Jan et al., 2011.

claim: RNAseq limitations include spurious antisense and splicing events produced by RT template switching.
source: RNAseq reveals diverse features of transcriptomes, but limitations can include misidentification of 3′ ends through internal priming (Jan et al., 2011), spurious antisense and splicing events produced by RT template switching (Houseley and Tollervey, 2010; Mourão et al., 2019), and the inability to detect all base modifications in the copying process (Helm and Motorin, 2017).
evidence: This limitation is cited with references to Houseley and Tollervey, 2010; Mourão et al., 2019.

claim: RNAseq has the inability to detect all base modifications in the copying process.
source: RNAseq reveals diverse features of transcriptomes, but limitations can include misidentification of 3′ ends through internal priming (Jan et al., 2011), spurious antisense and splicing events produced by RT template switching (Houseley and Tollervey, 2010; Mourão et al., 2019), and the inability to detect all base modifications in the copying process (Helm and Motorin, 2017).
evidence: This limitation is cited with reference to Helm and Motorin, 2017.

claim: The fragmentation of RNA prior to short-read sequencing makes it difficult to interpret the combination of authentic RNA processing events.
source: The fragmentation of RNA prior to short-read sequencing makes it difficult to interpret the combination of authentic RNA processing events and remains an unsolved problem (Steijger et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited with reference to Steijger et al., 2013.

claim: In nanopore DRS, the protein pore (nanopore) sits in a membrane through which an electrical current is passed, and intact RNA is fed through the nanopore by a motor protein.
source: In nanopore DRS, the protein pore (nanopore) sits in a membrane through which an electrical current is passed, and intact RNA is fed through the nanopore by a motor protein (Garalde et al., 2018).
evidence: This describes the nanopore DRS technology with citation to Garalde et al., 2018.

claim: Each RNA sequence within the nanopore (five bases) can be identified by the magnitude of signal it produces.
source: Each RNA sequence within the nanopore (five bases) can be identified by the magnitude of signal it produces.
evidence: This describes a technical feature of nanopore sequencing.

claim: Nanopore DRS and Illumina RNAseq were applied to wild-type Arabidopsis (Col-0) and mutants defective in m6A and exosome-mediated RNA decay.
source: We applied nanopore DRS and Illumina RNAseq to wild-type Arabidopsis (Col-0) and mutants defective in m6A (Růžička et al., 2017) and exosome-mediated RNA decay (Lange et al., 2014).
evidence: This describes the experimental design with citations to the mutant sources.

claim: The longest read alignment was 12.7 kb for mRNA transcribed from AT1G48090, spanning 63 exons.
source: The longest read alignments were 12.7 kb for mRNA transcribed from AT1G48090, spanning 63 exons, (Figure 1A), and 12.8 kb for mRNA transcribed from AT1G67120, spanning 58 exons (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: A 12.8 kb read alignment was detected for mRNA transcribed from AT1G67120, spanning 58 exons.
source: The longest read alignments were 12.7 kb for mRNA transcribed from AT1G48090, spanning 63 exons, (Figure 1A), and 12.8 kb for mRNA transcribed from AT1G67120, spanning 58 exons (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The 12.7 kb and 12.8 kb reads represent some of the longest contiguous mRNAs sequenced from Arabidopsis.
source: These represent some of the longest contiguous mRNAs sequenced from Arabidopsis.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the long read data.

claim: Among the shortest read alignments were those spanning genes encoding highly structured non-coding RNAs such as UsnRNAs and snoRNAs.
source: Among the shortest read alignments were those spanning genes encoding highly structured non-coding RNAs such as UsnRNAs and snoRNAs, for example U3B (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Synthetic ERCC RNA spike-ins were detected in a quantitative manner.
source: The spike-ins were detected in a quantitative manner (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), consistent with the suggestion that nanopore sequencing is quantitative (Garalde et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and cited to Garalde et al., 2018.

claim: For the portion of reads that align to the reference, sequence identity was 92% when measured against the ERCC RNA spike-ins.
source: For the portion of reads that align to the reference, sequence identity was 92% when measured against the ERCC RNA spike-ins (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The errors in nanopore sequencing showed evidence of base specificity.
source: The errors showed evidence of base specificity (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1D,E.

claim: Guanine was under-represented and uracil over-represented in indels and substitutions relative to the reference nucleotide distribution.
source: For example, guanine was under-represented and uracil over-represented in indels and substitutions relative to the reference nucleotide (nt) distribution.
evidence: This is stated as an example of base-specific errors.

claim: Proovread software tool and parallel Illumina RNAseq data were used to correct base-calling errors in the nanopore reads.
source: We used the proovread software tool (Hackl et al., 2014) and parallel Illumina RNAseq data to correct base-calling errors in the nanopore reads (Depledge et al., 2019).
evidence: This describes the error correction methodology with citations.

claim: Artefacts were detected caused by the MinKNOW software splitting raw signal from single molecules into two or more reads.
source: We detected artefacts caused by the MinKNOW software splitting raw signal from single molecules into two or more reads.
evidence: This describes an artifact observed in the data.

claim: Over-splitting in nanopore DRS generally occurs at low frequency (< 2% of reads).
source: Over-splitting in nanopore DRS generally occurs at low frequency (< 2% of reads).
evidence: This quantifies the frequency of the over-splitting artifact.

claim: RNAs originating from specific gene loci, such as RH3 (AT5G26742), appear to be more susceptible to over-splitting, with up to 20% of reads affected across multiple sequencing experiments.
source: However, RNAs originating from specific gene loci, such as RH3 (AT5G26742), appear to be more susceptible, with up to 20% of reads affected across multiple sequencing experiments (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This describes a specific example of over-splitting with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Two out of 9,445 (0.02%) reads mapped antisense to the ERCC RNA spike-in collection.
source: Two out of 9,445 (0.02%) reads mapped antisense to the ERCC RNA spike-in collection (Jiang et al., 2011).
evidence: This quantifies spurious antisense reads with citation to the ERCC collection.

claim: None of 19,665 reads mapped antisense to the highly expressed gene RUBISCO ACTIVASE (RCA) (AT2G39730).
source: None of 19,665 reads mapped antisense to the highly expressed gene RUBISCO ACTIVASE (RCA) (AT2G39730), consistent with the lack of antisense RNAs annotated at this locus.
evidence: This quantifies the absence of spurious antisense reads at a specific locus.

claim: Spurious antisense is rare or absent from nanopore DRS data.
source: Consequently, we conclude that spurious antisense is rare or absent from nanopore DRS data (Wyman, 2019; Mourão et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion with citations.

claim: Nanopore DRS can identify Arabidopsis long non-coding antisense RNAs, such as those at the auxin efflux carriers PIN4 and PIN7.
source: For example, by nanopore DRS, we could identify Arabidopsis long non-coding antisense RNAs, such as those at the auxin efflux carriers PIN4 and PIN7 (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is stated with reference to figures showing the data.

claim: The existence of previously unannotated antisense RNAs at PIN4 and PIN7 was supported by Illumina RNAseq of wild-type Col-0 and the exosome mutant hen2–2.
source: The existence of these previously unannotated antisense RNAs was supported by Illumina RNAseq of wild-type Col-0 and the exosome mutant hen2-2 (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1G) (Supplementary file 2A), the latter of which had a 13-fold increase in abundance of these antisense RNAs.
evidence: This is stated with reference to figures and supplementary data.

claim: The exosome mutant hen2-2 had a 13-fold increase in abundance of antisense RNAs at PIN4 and PIN7.
source: The existence of these previously unannotated antisense RNAs was supported by Illumina RNAseq of wild-type Col-0 and the exosome mutant hen2-2 (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1G) (Supplementary file 2A), the latter of which had a 13-fold increase in abundance of these antisense RNAs.
evidence: This quantifies the increase in antisense RNA abundance in the mutant.

claim: Ligation of the motor protein adapter to RNA 3′ ends results in nanopores sequencing mRNA poly(A) tails first.
source: Ligation of the motor protein adapter to RNA 3′ ends results in nanopores sequencing mRNA poly(A) tails first.
evidence: This describes a technical feature of the nanopore DRS protocol.

claim: Nanopolish-polyA software tool was used to estimate poly(A) tail lengths for individual reads.
source: We used the nanopolish-polyA software tool to estimate poly(A) tail lengths for individual reads (Workman et al., 2019).
evidence: This describes the computational method used with citation.

claim: ERCC-00002 has an expected poly(A) tail length of 24 nt, and the median nanopolish polyA estimate was 23.3 nt (95% confidence intervals [5.7, 102]; n = 1,485).
source: ERCC-00002 has an expected poly(A) tail length of 24 nt, and the median nanopolish polyA estimate was 23.3 nt (95% confidence intervals [CIs] [5.7, 102]; n = 1,485).
evidence: This validates the poly(A) tail length estimation method using a control.

claim: ERCC-00074 has an expected poly(A) tail length of 24 nt, and the median nanopolish-polyA estimate was 27.4 nt (95% CIs [8.9, 118]; n = 1,439).
source: ERCC-00074 also has an expected poly(A) tail length of 24 nt, and the median nanopolish-polyA estimate was 27.4 nt (95% CIs [8.9, 118]; n = 1,439).
evidence: This validates the poly(A) tail length estimation method using another control.

claim: The median nanopolish-polyA estimates of poly(A) tail length are accurate within a few bases, but individual read measurements have a wide margin of error.
source: We conclude that the median nanopolish-polyA estimates of poly(A) tail length are accurate within a few bases, but individual read measurements have a wide margin of error.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the validation experiments.

claim: The median length estimate for Arabidopsis mRNA poly(A) tails is 68 nt, with a wide range in estimated lengths for individual mRNAs (95% were in the 13–200 nt range).
source: Application of this approach to reads mapping to the Arabidopsis genome indicated a median length estimate of 68 nt for Arabidopsis mRNA poly(A) tails, but with a wide range in estimated lengths for individual mRNAs (95% were in the 13–200 nt range; Figure 2A).
evidence: This quantifies poly(A) tail lengths in Arabidopsis with reference to Figure 2A.

claim: Chloroplast-encoded transcripts have a median poly(A) tail length of 13 nt (95% CIs [3.1, 56]).
source: The generally shorter poly(A) tails of chloroplast- (median length 13 nt, 95% CIs [3.1, 56]) and mitochondria-encoded (median length 20 nt, 95% CIs [4.1, 73] transcripts, which are a feature of RNA decay in these organelles, were also detectable.
evidence: This quantifies poly(A) tail lengths for chloroplast transcripts.

claim: Mitochondria-encoded transcripts have a median poly(A) tail length of 20 nt (95% CIs [4.1, 73]).
source: The generally shorter poly(A) tails of chloroplast- (median length 13 nt, 95% CIs [3.1, 56]) and mitochondria-encoded (median length 20 nt, 95% CIs [4.1, 73] transcripts, which are a feature of RNA decay in these organelles, were also detectable.
evidence: This quantifies poly(A) tail lengths for mitochondrial transcripts.

claim: Poly(A) tail length correlates negatively (Spearman's ρ = −0.34, p < 1 × 10−16, 95% CIs [−0.36,–0.32]) with gene expression in Arabidopsis.
source: We find that poly(A) tail length correlates negatively (Spearman's ρ = −0.34, p < 1 × 10−16, 95% CIs [−0.36,–0.32]) with gene expression in Arabidopsis (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), consistent with other species analysed by short-read TAILseq (Lima et al., 2017).
evidence: This reports a statistical correlation with reference to a figure and citation.

claim: The median genomic distance between nanopore DRS and Helicos DRS 3′ ends was 0 ± 13 nt (one standard deviation).
source: The median genomic distance between nanopore DRS and Helicos DRS 3′ ends was 0 ± 13 nt (one standard deviation) demonstrating close agreement between these orthogonal technologies (Figure 2B).
evidence: This quantifies the agreement between two sequencing technologies with reference to Figure 2B.

claim: 97% of nanopore DRS 3′ ends (4,152,800 reads at 639,178 unique sites, 93% of all unique sites) mapped to either annotated 3′ untranslated regions (UTRs) or downstream of the current annotation.
source: For example, 97% of nanopore DRS 3′ ends (4,152,800 reads at 639,178 unique sites, 93% of all unique sites) mapped to either annotated 3′ untranslated regions (UTRs) or downstream of the current annotation.
evidence: This quantifies the distribution of 3' ends.

claim: Mapping of 3′ ends to coding sequences or 5′UTRs was rare (2.8%, 119,524 reads at 39,610 unique sites, 5.8% of all unique sites).
source: Mapping of 3′ ends to coding sequences or 5′UTRs was rare (2.8%, 119,524 reads at 39,610 unique sites, 5.8% of all unique sites), and mapping to introns even rarer (0.29%, 12,554 reads at 7791 unique sites, 1.1% of unique sites).
evidence: This quantifies the rare occurrence of 3' ends in coding sequences or 5'UTRs.

claim: Mapping of 3′ ends to introns was even rarer (0.29%, 12,554 reads at 7791 unique sites, 1.1% of unique sites).
source: Mapping of 3′ ends to coding sequences or 5′UTRs was rare (2.8%, 119,524 reads at 39,610 unique sites, 5.8% of all unique sites), and mapping to introns even rarer (0.29%, 12,554 reads at 7791 unique sites, 1.1% of unique sites).
evidence: This quantifies the rare occurrence of 3' ends in introns.

claim: Alternative polyadenylation in mRNA encoding the RNA-binding protein FPA controls flowering time.
source: Even so, examples of the latter included sites of alternative polyadenylation with well-established regulatory roles, such as in mRNA encoding the RNA-binding protein FPA, which controls flowering time (Hornyik et al., 2010) (Figure 2C), and in mRNA encoding the histone H3K9 demethylase IBM1, which controls levels of genic DNA methylation (Rigal et al., 2012) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Hornyik et al., 2010 and reference to Figure 2C.

claim: Alternative polyadenylation in mRNA encoding the histone H3K9 demethylase IBM1 controls levels of genic DNA methylation.
source: Even so, examples of the latter included sites of alternative polyadenylation with well-established regulatory roles, such as in mRNA encoding the RNA-binding protein FPA, which controls flowering time (Hornyik et al., 2010) (Figure 2C), and in mRNA encoding the histone H3K9 demethylase IBM1, which controls levels of genic DNA methylation (Rigal et al., 2012) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Rigal et al., 2012 and reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Cleavage and polyadenylation within PTM intron 10 terminates transcripts prior to sequence encoding the transmembrane domain, bypassing established retrograde control.
source: Cleavage and polyadenylation within PTM intron 10 (supported by our Helicos DRS data) terminates transcripts prior to sequence encoding the transmembrane domain, hence bypassing established retrograde control.
evidence: This describes a novel finding about PTM regulation.

claim: Of the 10,116 oligo(A)6 sequences in coding sequences, only four have read alignments terminating within 13 nt in all four datasets.
source: Of the 10,116 such oligo(A)6 sequences, only four have read alignments terminating within 13 nt in all four datasets.
evidence: This quantifies the absence of internal priming artifacts.

claim: Internal priming is rare or absent in nanopore DRS data.
source: Hence, internal priming is rare or absent in nanopore DRS data.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the internal priming analysis.

claim: Nanopore DRS reads are frequently truncated prior to annotated transcription start sites, resulting in a 3′ bias of genomic alignments.
source: Nanopore DRS reads are frequently truncated prior to annotated transcription start sites, resulting in a 3′ bias of genomic alignments (Figure 3A) (Depledge et al., 2019).
evidence: This describes a limitation of nanopore DRS with citation and reference to Figure 3A.

claim: Cap-dependent ligation of a biotinylated 5′ adapter RNA was used to purify capped mRNAs.
source: To address this issue, we used cap-dependent ligation of a biotinylated 5′ adapter RNA to purify capped mRNAs (a related approach has recently been used by others Jiang et al., 2019).
evidence: This describes a methodological approach with citation to Jiang et al., 2019.

claim: 5′ adapter RNA ligation reduced the median 3′ bias of nanopore read alignments per gene from 0.45 (95% CIs [0.43,0.47]) to 0.08 (95% CIs [0.07,0.09]).
source: This procedure reduced the median 3′ bias of nanopore read alignments per gene (as measured by quartile coefficient of variation of per base coverage) from 0.45 (95% CIs [0.43,0.47]) to 0.08 (95% CIs [0.07,0.09]; Figure 3B).
evidence: This quantifies the improvement in 3' bias with reference to Figure 3B.

claim: 41% of adapter-ligated nanopore DRS reads mapped within 5 nt of transcription start sites identified from full-length Arabidopsis cDNA clones.
source: We found that 41% of adapter-ligated nanopore DRS reads mapped within 5 nt of transcription start sites and 60% mapped within 13 nt (Figure 3C).
evidence: This quantifies the accuracy of 5' end detection with reference to Figure 3C.

claim: 60% of adapter-ligated nanopore DRS reads mapped within 13 nt of transcription start sites identified from full-length Arabidopsis cDNA clones.
source: We found that 41% of adapter-ligated nanopore DRS reads mapped within 5 nt of transcription start sites and 60% mapped within 13 nt (Figure 3C).
evidence: This quantifies the accuracy of 5' end detection with reference to Figure 3C.

claim: 75% of nanopore DRS cap-capture 5' ends mapped within 5 nt of a transcription start site detected using nanoPARE.
source: We found that 75% of nanopore DRS cap-capture 5' ends mapped within 5 nt of a transcription start site detected using single base resolution peak-calling from nanoPARE reads, and 82% mapped with 13 nt (Figure 3C).
evidence: This quantifies the accuracy of 5' end detection compared to nanoPARE with reference to Figure 3C.

claim: 82% of nanopore DRS cap-capture 5' ends mapped within 13 nt of a transcription start site detected using nanoPARE.
source: We found that 75% of nanopore DRS cap-capture 5' ends mapped within 5 nt of a transcription start site detected using single base resolution peak-calling from nanoPARE reads, and 82% mapped with 13 nt (Figure 3C).
evidence: This quantifies the accuracy of 5' end detection compared to nanoPARE with reference to Figure 3C.

claim: Reads with adapters had, on average, 11 nt more at their 5′ ends that could be aligned to the genome compared with reads lacking the 5′ adapter RNA.
source: Reads with adapters had, on average, 11 nt more at their 5′ ends that could be aligned to the genome compared with the most common 5′ alignment position of reads lacking the 5′ adapter RNA (Figure 3D).
evidence: This quantifies the improvement in 5' end detection with reference to Figure 3D.

claim: The 5′ end of RNA is not correctly sequenced due to loss of processive control by the motor protein when the end of an RNA molecule enters the pore.
source: This difference may be explained by loss of processive control by the motor protein when the end of an RNA molecule enters the pore.
evidence: This is stated as an explanation for the loss of 5' sequence.

claim: Reads mapping to the synthetic ERCC RNA Spike-Ins and in vitro transcribed RNAs lacked ~11 nt of authentic 5′ sequence.
source: Consistent with these Arabidopsis transcriptome-wide nanopore DRS data, reads mapping to the synthetic ERCC RNA Spike-Ins and in vitro transcribed RNAs also lacked ~11 nt of authentic 5′ sequence (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E,F).
evidence: This validates the 5' truncation observation using controls with reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 1E,F.

claim: The apparent overestimation of 5′UTR length is widespread in Araport11 annotation.
source: The apparent overestimation of 5′UTR length is widespread in Araport11 annotation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G), consistent with the assessment of capped Arabidopsis 5′ ends detected by nanoPARE sequencing (Schon et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated with reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 1G and citation to Schon et al., 2018.

claim: Nanopore DRS can reveal regions of internal mRNA and ncRNA cleavage.
source: Therefore, nanopore DRS can reveal regions of internal mRNA and ncRNA cleavage.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the miRNA cleavage analysis.

claim: 58% (170,702) of the unique splice junctions detected in the combined set of replicate data were absent from Araport11 and AtRTD2 annotations and were unsupported by Illumina RNAseq.
source: However, a combination of base-calling and alignment errors contributed to the misidentification of splicing events for uncorrected DRS data: 58% (170,702) of the unique splice junctions detected in the combined set of replicate data were absent from Araport11 and AtRTD2 annotations and were unsupported by Illumina RNAseq (Figure 4B, Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This quantifies the error rate in splice junction detection before error correction with reference to Figure 4B and Supplementary file 5.

claim: After error correction, only 13% (39,061) of unique splice junctions were unsupported by an orthogonal dataset.
source: After error correction, only 13% (39,061) of unique splice junctions were unsupported by an orthogonal dataset, consistent with an improvement in alignment accuracy.
evidence: This quantifies the improvement in splice junction detection after error correction.

claim: The four nanopore DRS datasets for Col-0 biological replicates captured 75% (102,486) of Araport11 splice site annotations.
source: The four nanopore DRS datasets for Col-0 biological replicates captured 75% (102,486) and 69% (104,686) of Araport11 and AtRTD2 splice site annotations, respectively.
evidence: This quantifies the coverage of annotated splice sites.

claim: The four nanopore DRS datasets for Col-0 biological replicates captured 69% (104,686) of AtRTD2 splice site annotations.
source: The four nanopore DRS datasets for Col-0 biological replicates captured 75% (102,486) and 69% (104,686) of Araport11 and AtRTD2 splice site annotations, respectively.
evidence: This quantifies the coverage of annotated splice sites.

claim: 100,450 (81%) canonical GU/AG splicing events detected in the error-corrected nanopore data were found in both Araport11 and AtRTD2 annotations and were supported by Illumina RNAseq.
source: Most of the canonical GU/AG splicing events (100,450; 81%) detected in the error-corrected nanopore data were found in both annotations and were supported by Illumina RNAseq (Figure 4B, Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This quantifies the validated splice junctions with reference to Figure 4B and Supplementary file 5.

claim: 3,234 unique canonical splicing events in the error-corrected nanopore DRS data were supported by Illumina RNAseq but absent from both Araport11 and AtRTD2 annotations.
source: A total of 3,234 unique canonical splicing events in the error-corrected nanopore DRS data were supported by Illumina RNAseq but absent from both Araport11 and AtRTD2 annotations, highlighting potential gaps in our understanding of the complexity of Arabidopsis splicing annotation (Figure 4B, Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This quantifies novel splice junctions with reference to Figure 4B and Supplementary file 5.

claim: Of the 3,234 novel GU/AG events found in error-corrected data and supported by Illumina alignments, 74% were classified as canonical U2 or U12 splice sites.
source: Of the 3,234 novel GU/AG events found in error-corrected data and supported by Illumina alignments, 74% were classified as canonical U2 or U12 splice sites, suggesting that they are authentic (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This quantifies the classification of novel splice sites with reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: 19 FLM splicing patterns were identified that adhered to known splice junction sites, but 11 of these transcript isoforms were not previously annotated.
source: For example, we identified 19 FLM splicing patterns that adhered to known splice junction sites (Figure 4A). However, 11 of these transcript isoforms were not previously annotated.
evidence: This quantifies novel isoforms at FLM with reference to Figure 4A.

claim: 13,064 unique splicing patterns were detected that matched annotations in Araport11, AtRTD2 or both.
source: In total, 13,064 unique splicing patterns were detected that matched annotations in Araport11, AtRTD2 or both (Figure 4C).
evidence: This quantifies annotated splicing patterns with reference to Figure 4C.

claim: 8,659 unique splicing patterns were identified that were not present in either Araport11 or AtRTD2 annotation.
source: Another 8,659 unique splicing patterns were identified that were not present in either annotation (Figure 4C, Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This quantifies novel splicing patterns with reference to Figure 4C and Supplementary file 5.

claim: Of the 8,659 novel splicing patterns, 50% (4,293) used only splice donor and acceptor pairs that were already annotated in either Araport11 or AtRTD2.
source: Of these, 50% (4,293) used only splice donor and acceptor pairs that were already annotated in either Araport11 or AtRTD2.
evidence: This quantifies novel combinations of known splice sites.

claim: 17,491 sites with a more than two-fold higher error rate were identified in the VIR-complemented line with restored m6A compared to the vir-1 mutant.
source: We identified 17,491 sites with a more than two-fold higher error rate (compared with the TAIR10 reference base) in the VIR-complemented line with restored m6A (Figure 5A).
evidence: This quantifies differential error sites with reference to Figure 5A.

claim: 99.4% of the differential error sites mapped within Araport11 annotated protein-coding genes.
source: In all, 99.4% of the differential error sites mapped within Araport11 annotated protein-coding genes.
evidence: This quantifies the distribution of differential error sites.

claim: Motif analysis of differential error sites revealed the DRAYH (D = G or U or A, R = G or A, Y = C or U, H = A or C or U) sequence (E value < 1 × 10−16), which closely resembles the established m6A target consensus.
source: Motif analysis of these error sites revealed the DRAYH (D = G or U or A, R = G or A, Y = C or U, H = A or C or U) sequence (E value < 1 × 10−16), which closely resembles the established m6A target consensus (Meyer and Jaffrey, 2017; Roundtree et al., 2017) (Figure 5B).
evidence: This describes the motif analysis with citations and reference to Figure 5B.

claim: The most frequently detected motifs in the nanopore DRS analysis, AAm6ACU and AAm6ACA, match those most frequently detected in Arabidopsis using the orthogonal Me-RIP approach.
source: The most frequently detected motifs in this analysis, AAm6ACU and AAm6ACA (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), match those most frequently detected in Arabidopsis using the orthogonal Me-RIP approach (Luo et al., 2014).
evidence: This validates the motif findings with citation to Luo et al., 2014 and reference to Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: 187 sites (4.8%) were detected associated with the motif AGAUU, raising the possibility that a C following m6A is not an invariant feature of the Arabidopsis m6A code.
source: Notably, we also detect 187 sites (4.8%) associated with the motif AGAUU (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), raising the possibility that a C following m6A is not an invariant feature of the Arabidopsis m6A code.
evidence: This describes a novel finding about the m6A motif with reference to Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The error sites were preferentially found in 3′UTRs.
source: In addition, like the established location of m6A sites in mRNAs (Meyer and Jaffrey, 2017; Roundtree et al., 2017), the error sites were preferentially found in 3′UTRs (Figure 5C).
evidence: This describes the distribution of error sites with citations and reference to Figure 5C.

claim: 66% of the called nanopore DRS differential error sites fell within 5 nt of an miCLIP peak.
source: In all, 66% of the called nanopore DRS differential error sites fell within 5 nt of an miCLIP peak (Figure 5E,F).
evidence: This validates the nanopore m6A detection with miCLIP data with reference to Figure 5E,F.

claim: When 50% of reads in the methylation positive condition are sampled from the unmethylated condition, more than 200 reads per condition are required to reliably detect m6A in > 95% bootstraps.
source: When 50% of reads in the methylation positive condition are sampled from the unmethylated condition, more than 200 reads per condition are required to reliably detect m6A in > 95% bootstraps, indicating that stoichiometry is an important factor in the power to detect differentially methylated sites (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This quantifies the sequencing depth requirements with reference to Figure 5—figure supplement 1E.

claim: A global reduction in protein-coding gene expression was found in vir-1, corresponding to transcripts that were methylated in the VIR-complemented line.
source: We found a global reduction in protein-coding gene expression in vir-1 (using either nanopore DRS or Illumina RNAseq data), corresponding to transcripts that were methylated in the VIR-complemented line (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This describes the impact of m6A loss on gene expression with reference to Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: m6A predominantly protects Arabidopsis mRNAs from endonucleolytic cleavage.
source: These findings are consistent with the recent discovery that m6A predominantly protects Arabidopsis mRNAs from endonucleolytic cleavage (Anderson et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Anderson et al., 2018.

claim: m6A predominantly promotes mRNA decay in human cells.
source: Therefore, although the m6A writer complex comprises conserved components that target a conserved consensus sequence and distribution of m6A is enriched in the last exon, it appears that this modification predominantly promotes mRNA decay in human cells (Wang et al., 2014), but mRNA stability in Arabidopsis (Anderson et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Wang et al., 2014 and Anderson et al., 2018.

claim: m6A promotes mRNA stability in Arabidopsis.
source: Therefore, although the m6A writer complex comprises conserved components that target a conserved consensus sequence and distribution of m6A is enriched in the last exon, it appears that this modification predominantly promotes mRNA decay in human cells (Wang et al., 2014), but mRNA stability in Arabidopsis (Anderson et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Anderson et al., 2018.

claim: The vir-1 mutant had a lengthened clock period.
source: This distinction was associated with a biological consequence in that the vir-1 mutant had a lengthened clock period (Figure 6B,C).
evidence: This describes a phenotype with reference to Figure 6B,C.

claim: m6A was detected at mRNAs encoding the clock components PRR7, GI and LNK1/2 in both the nanopore DRS and miCLIP data.
source: We detected m6A at mRNAs encoding the clock components PRR7, GI and LNK1/2 in both the nanopore DRS and miCLIP data (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This describes m6A detection at specific genes with reference to Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: vir-1 mutants had reduced abundance of CAB1 mRNAs with 20 and 40 nt poly(A) tails, and an increased abundance of poly(A) tails of 60 nt in length.
source: vir-1 mutants had reduced abundance of CAB1 mRNAs with 20 and 40 nt poly(A) tails, and an increased abundance of poly(A) tails of 60 nt in length (Figure 6D).
evidence: This describes changes in poly(A) tail length distribution with reference to Figure 6D.

claim: FLOWERING LOCUS C (FLC) expression was reduced by more than 40-fold compared with the wild type in vir-1.
source: Notably, FLOWERING LOCUS C (FLC) expression was reduced by more than 40-fold compared with the wild type (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This quantifies gene expression change with reference to Figure 6—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Detectable disruptions to splicing in vir-1 were modest.
source: Detectable disruptions to splicing in vir-1 were modest.
evidence: This describes the limited impact on splicing.

claim: A clear defect in RNA 3′ end formation in vir-1 was apparent.
source: In contrast, a clear defect in RNA 3′ end formation in vir-1 was apparent.
evidence: This describes a major impact on 3' end formation.

claim: 3,579 genes (FDR < 0.05, absolute change in position of > 13 nt) had an altered nanopore DRS 3′ position profile in the vir-1 mutant compared with the VIR-complemented line.
source: Using a Kolmogorov–Smirnov test, we identified 3,579 genes (FDR < 0.05, absolute change in position of > 13 nt) with an altered nanopore DRS 3′ position profile in the vir-1 mutant compared with the VIR-complemented line (Figure 7A).
evidence: This quantifies genes with altered 3' end profiles with reference to Figure 7A.

claim: 3,008 genes displayed a shift to usage of more proximal poly(A) sites in vir-1.
source: Of these, 3,008 displayed a shift to usage of more proximal poly(A) sites in vir-1: 59% of these genes also contain m6A sites detectable by nanopore DRS (compared with 32% of all expressed genes, p < 1 × 10−16; 61% were detectable by miCLIP compared with 35% of all expressed genes, p < 1 × 10−16) and correspond to locations of increased cleavage downstream of m6A sites in the vir-1 mutant (Figure 7B).
evidence: This quantifies the shift to proximal poly(A) sites with reference to Figure 7B.

claim: 571 genes showed increased transcriptional readthrough beyond the 3′ end in vir-1.
source: A total of 571 genes showed increased transcriptional readthrough beyond the 3′ end in vir-1 (Figure 7A): 72% of these loci also contained nanopore-mapped m6A sites (p < 1 × 10−16; 71% were detectable by miCLIP, p < 1 × 10−16).
evidence: This quantifies readthrough events with reference to Figure 7A.

claim: 327 error sites were phased with 3' end position, overlapping 207 annotated genes.
source: We identified 327 error sites which were phased with 3' end position, overlapping 207 annotated genes.
evidence: This quantifies the phasing of m6A with poly(A) sites.

claim: 149 (72%) of the 207 genes with phased error sites also display a statistically detectable change in 3' end position in the vir-1 mutant compared to VIRc.
source: 149 (72%) of these also display a statistically detectable change in 3' end position in the vir-1 mutant compared to VIRc.
evidence: This quantifies the overlap between phased sites and altered 3' ends.

claim: The distribution of the canonical poly(A) signal AAUAAA peaks 19 nt upstream of the cleavage site in Arabidopsis mRNA.
source: Notably, the distribution of the canonical poly(A) signal AAUAAA peaks 19 nt upstream of the cleavage site in Arabidopsis mRNA (related hexamers, differing at only a single position, show similar distribution patterns) (Sherstnev et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Sherstnev et al., 2012.

claim: The peak of AAUAAA-like poly(A) signals closely overlaps with the m6A motif.
source: This analysis reveals a close overlap of the peak of AAUAAA-like poly(A) signals with the m6A motif (Figure 7E).
evidence: This describes the spatial relationship between poly(A) signals and m6A with reference to Figure 7E.

claim: Adenosine residues directly adjacent to, or within, the poly(A) signal itself may be methylated.
source: This finding may reflect the relative similarity of the most common Arabidopsis m6A motifs (such as AAACU and AAACA) to the poly(A) signal, and indicates that adenosine residues directly adjacent to, or within, the poly(A) signal itself may be methylated.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the overlap between m6A and poly(A) signals.

claim: Loss of m6A activates the selection of upstream poly(A) signals.
source: Since loss of m6A activates the selection of upstream poly(A) signals, these findings are consistent with m6A at (or in the vicinity of) AAUAAA inhibiting recognition of the poly(A) signal for subsequent cleavage and polyadenylation.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the functional role of m6A.

claim: 523 loci with increased levels of chimeric RNAs in vir-1 were detected resulting from unterminated transcription proceeding into downstream genes on the same strand.
source: We detected 523 loci with increased levels of chimeric RNAs in vir-1 resulting from unterminated transcription proceeding into downstream genes on the same strand (Supplementary dataset 24).
evidence: This quantifies chimeric RNA formation with reference to supplementary data.

claim: Only 33% of upstream genes forming the chimeric RNAs had detectable m6A sites in the VIR-complemented line with restored VIR activity.
source: However, only 33% of upstream genes forming the chimeric RNAs had detectable m6A sites in the VIR-complemented line with restored VIR activity.
evidence: This quantifies the proportion of chimeric RNA genes with m6A.

claim: Loss of VIRILIZER-dependent m6A disrupts Arabidopsis mRNA 3' formation.
source: Overall, we conclude that loss of VIRILIZER-dependent m6A disrupts Arabidopsis mRNA 3' formation.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the 3' end analysis.

claim: The predominant impact of m6A loss is loss of suppression of proximal poly(A) sites.
source: Although this includes readthrough at poly(A) sites with the formation of chimeric RNAs, the predominant impact is loss of suppression of proximal poly(A) sites.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the 3' end analysis.

claim: Nanopore DRS can identify multiple authentic features of RNA 3′ end processing.
source: Hence, internal priming is rare or absent in nanopore DRS data. It is possible that a standard nanopore DRS approach may be compromised in the quantitative detection of RNAs with very short poly(A) tails or tails incorporating uridylation for decay. However, overall, we conclude that nanopore DRS can identify multiple authentic features of RNA 3′ end processing.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the 3' end analysis.

claim: Improvements in the utility of nanopore DRS likely depend upon more accurate base-calling, refined splitting of signal, increased read-depth and the development of software for splice-aware alignment of long sequencing reads.
source: Improvements in the utility of nanopore DRS likely depend upon more accurate base-calling, refined splitting of signal, increased read-depth and the development of software for splice-aware alignment of long sequencing reads.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion about future improvements.

claim: A simple and transparent statistical test of basecalling error rate can identify m6A.
source: We show that a simple and transparent statistical test of basecalling error rate can identify m6A.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion about the m6A detection method.

claim: Antibody-based approaches such as MeRIP/m6A-seq and miCLIP cannot readily define stoichiometry, do not necessarily detect m6A only, have unclear sensitivity, and the fragmentation of RNA required for library preparation may result in the underrepresentation of sites close to RNA 3' ends.
source: However, antibody-based approaches such as MeRIP/m6A-seq and miCLIP are limited in some respects. For example, they cannot readily define stoichiometry, do not necessarily detect m6A only, have unclear sensitivity, and the fragmentation of RNA required for library preparation may result in the underrepresentation of sites close to RNA 3' ends.
evidence: This describes limitations of antibody-based methods.

claim: MAZTER-Seq is limited to the detection of m6As in an ACA context and the majority of m6A sites in human or yeast cells cannot be detected.
source: Since MAZTER-Seq is limited to the detection of m6As in an ACA context (and spatial constraints) the majority of m6A sites in human or yeast cells cannot be detected (Garcia-Campos et al., 2019).
evidence: This describes a limitation of MAZTER-Seq with citation to Garcia-Campos et al., 2019.

claim: EpiNano cannot currently call m6A in a k-mer with more than one adenosine, and hence 92% of m6A sites identified in Arabidopsis are undetectable with this approach.
source: However, EpiNano cannot currently call m6A in a k-mer with more than one adenosine, and hence 92% of m6A sites we identify in Arabidopsis are undetectable with this approach (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E) (Liu et al., 2019).
evidence: This describes a limitation of EpiNano with citation to Liu et al., 2019 and reference to Figure 5—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Disrupting m6A was associated with altered patterns of mRNA cleavage and polyadenylation.
source: The key biological question we set out to address, was whether an unbiased transcriptome-wide sequencing approach (that mapped m6A in the context of full-length mRNAs) could reveal the functional impacts of m6A on Arabidopsis gene expression. We found that disrupting m6A was associated with altered patterns of mRNA cleavage and polyadenylation.
evidence: This is stated as a key finding.

claim: m6A can suppress proximal poly(A) site selection.
source: Although we detected readthrough at some poly(A) sites, the predominant effect was the activation of proximal poly(A) sites in the absence of m6A, indicating that m6A can suppress proximal poly(A) site selection.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the functional role of m6A.

claim: Arabidopsis expresses a CPSF30 isoform that encodes a YT521-B homology (YTH) domain with the potential to bind and read m6A.
source: Meanwhile, Arabidopsis (like other plants and the apicomplexa) expresses a CPSF30 isoform (regulated by alternative polyadenylation in Arabidopsis) that encodes a YT521-B homology (YTH) domain with the potential to bind and read m6A (Stevens et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Stevens et al., 2018.

claim: m6A is almost exclusively found in mRNA 3'UTRs in steady-state analyses.
source: The impact of individual m6A sites on Arabidopsis biology is likely to be context-specific. However, it is clear that m6A is almost exclusively found in mRNA 3'UTRs (in steady-state analyses).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the data.

claim: Arabidopsis has 13 YTH domain containing proteins with the potential to bind and read m6A.
source: Arabidopsis has 13 YTH domain containing proteins with the potential to bind and read m6A (Reichel et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Reichel et al., 2019.

claim: Nanopore DRS has the potential to refine multiple features of Arabidopsis genome annotation.
source: We have shown that nanopore DRS has the potential to refine multiple features of Arabidopsis genome annotation and to generate the clearest map to date of m6A locations, despite the genome sequence being available since 2000 (Kaul and Arabidopsis Genome Initiative, 2000).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion with citation to Kaul and Arabidopsis Genome Initiative, 2000.

claim: The combination of nanopore DRS and other sequencing approaches will improve genome annotation.
source: Based on our experience with Arabidopsis, we anticipate that the combination of nanopore DRS and other sequencing approaches will improve genome annotation.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion and prediction.
